notes: Court of Appeal dismissed VAT appeal; partnership land transfer via TR1 was supply by Fengate notwithstanding Box 12 additional provision.

enrichment.short_title: Fengate v Customs: VAT on partnership land transfer via TR1
key_facts: Fengate Developments, a VAT-registered property partnership, held Red Land vested in Mr and Mrs Darlow as beneficial joint tenants.

On 8 July 1999 the Darlows executed a Land Registry TR1 transferring the whole Red Land for stated consideration of £125,000 while two £125,000 payments totalling £250,000 were paid into the partnership account.
Customs assessed VAT on a taxable supply of the land at £37,234 plus interest after Fengate had waived exemption.
Box 12 of the TR1 stated the transfer related exclusively to Mrs Darlow's interest; the tribunal found a transfer of the whole partnership asset.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal second appeal from Evans-Lombe J dismissing Fengate's appeal from the VAT and Duties Tribunal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused; appellant ordered to pay costs of the appeal and the High Court appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Whether a partnership made a VAT supply of land is a question of fact on the whole transaction; the tribunal was entitled to construe the TR1 in context and find Fengate transferred the whole Red Land as a partnership asset for £250,000, notwithstanding Box 12 and unchallenged oral evidence of capital injections.
legal_issues: Whether Fengate made a taxable supply of land on transfer of the Red Land
Construction of Land Registry Form TR1 and Box 12 additional provision
Whether Schedule 10 paragraph 8 applies when grantor and consideration beneficiary differ
Whether tribunal findings on partnership accounts and bank payments were open on the evidence
linked_authorities: Customs & Excise Commissioners v Reed Personnel Services Ltd [1995] STC 588

confidence.notes: Full Court of Appeal judgment on TR1 construction and VAT supply with detailed tribunal findings.

notes: Chadwick LJ refused permission to appeal from Norris QC's dismissal of Rowleys' attempt to set aside section 50 LPA order.

enrichment.short_title: Barclays v Rowley: section 50 order not set aside
key_facts: Barclays obtained possession of 24 Eggington Road after mortgage proceedings concluded in 2001 against Mr and Mrs Rowley.
Barclays applied under section 50 LPA 1925 to sell freed from prior Halifax charges, lodging proceeds in court with an undertaking to cover any shortfall.
Mr Martin QC made the section 50 order in January 2004 without service on the Rowleys or Halifax.
The Rowleys sought to set aside the order; Judge Norris tested the application and dismissed it as having no prospect of success.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal application for permission to appeal from a High Court refusal to set aside a section 50 Law of Property Act order.
enrichment.outcome: Application for permission to appeal dismissed; no order as to costs.
enrichment.ratio: A section 50 order enabling a mortgagee to convey property freed from prior charges does not finally account between mortgagor and mortgagee or resolve disputes with prior chargees; it merely transfers security to money in court, and setting aside such an order after sale and conveyance is not available when disputes should be pursued by account or under the order's machinery.
legal_issues: Whether a section 50 order should be set aside for lack of notice to mortgagors
Whether Rowleys could challenge amounts due under the MacDuff possession judgment
Whether section 50 permits sale by a second mortgagee ahead of the first chargee
Whether the application to set aside was misconceived after the property was sold
linked_authorities: Barclays Bank plc v Rowley [2001] EWCA Civ 2040

confidence.notes: Clear permission judgment explaining section 50 mechanics and procedural history.

notes: Chadwick LJ refused second appeal against refusal to extend time to challenge bankruptcy annulment; limitation point hopeless.

enrichment.short_title: Ahmad v IR: no extension of time on hopeless limitation appeal
key_facts: The Inland Revenue served a statutory demand on Mr Ahmad for about £309,561 in tax liabilities in 2001.
His application to set aside the demand on limitation grounds was dismissed in June 2002 while an appeal remained pending.
A bankruptcy petition was presented and a bankruptcy order made in September 2002 before the limitation appeal was heard.
Mr Ahmad sought annulment and, out of time, to appeal the refusal to annul; Evans-Lombe J refused extension of time.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal application for permission to appeal (second appeal) from refusal to extend time to appeal a registrar's refusal to annul a bankruptcy order.
enrichment.outcome: Application for permission to appeal refused; no order as to costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where an out-of-time appeal against refusal to annul bankruptcy would only revive a hopeless limitation challenge to a statutory demand excluded from the Limitation Act by section 37(2), extending time serves no useful purpose and Re Noble justifies refusing extension even if other grounds might have been arguable.
legal_issues: Whether a pending appeal against refusal to set aside a statutory demand bars presenting a bankruptcy petition under section 267(2)(d)
Whether tax claims are subject to limitation under section 37(2) of the Limitation Act 1980
Whether time should be extended to appeal refusal to annul bankruptcy when underlying limitation point is hopeless
Whether CPR 52.13 second appeal criteria are met

confidence.notes: Detailed procedural history with clear refusal on Re Noble discretion and limitation analysis.

notes: Brief Court of Appeal order dismissing Fengate VAT appeal, refusing 50% costs reduction and House of Lords permission.

enrichment.short_title: Fengate v Customs: appeal dismissed; full costs and no HL permission
key_facts: The Court of Appeal dismissed Fengate Developments' VAT appeal for reasons in draft judgments circulated to counsel.
Fengate sought a 50% costs order rather than the normal unsuccessful appellant costs order.
Fengate also applied for permission to appeal to the House of Lords.
The court noted Fengate had lost at every stage and the appeal involved challenges to tribunal findings of fact.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal oral judgment on costs and permission following dismissal of Fengate's VAT appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; appellant to pay respondent's costs of the appeal and High Court appeal subject to detailed assessment; permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Following dismissal of a VAT appeal on draft judgments, the normal order is that the unsuccessful appellant pays full costs; a reduced costs order is inappropriate where the appellant has lost at every stage on fact-sensitive issues, and no point of general public importance warrants House of Lords permission.
legal_issues: Whether Fengate should pay only 50% of Customs' appeal costs
Whether permission to appeal to the House of Lords should be granted
linked_authorities: Fengate Developments (A Partnership) v Customs & Excise [2004] EWCA Civ 1591

confidence.notes: Short procedural order with clear outcomes on costs and permission; substantive ratio in EWCA Civ 1591.

notes: Court of Appeal partly allowed appeal; arbitration clause bound New India but anti-suit injunction against Finnish proceedings set aside.

enrichment.short_title: Through Transport v New India: arbitration and Brussels Regulation
key_facts: A container of garments was lost during carriage from Kotka, Finland to Moscow under through bills of lading and a CMR waybill.
The Club, as P&I insurer, sought contribution from New India under a reinsurance policy containing London arbitration clauses.
New India commenced proceedings in Finland under the Finnish Insurance Contracts Act after BMO's bankruptcy.
Moore-Bick J declared New India bound to arbitrate in England and granted an anti-suit injunction restraining Finnish proceedings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from Moore-Bick J on jurisdiction, arbitration, Brussels Regulation application, and anti-suit injunction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; declaration that New India must arbitrate in England upheld; declaration that Finnish proceedings were in breach of contract and anti-suit injunction set aside; costs split in court below and on appeal.
enrichment.ratio: Claims under the Brussels Regulation arbitration exception fall outside the Regulation and the court first seised in Finland could not determine that issue; English conflicts principles bound New India to arbitrate in London, but pursuing statutory rights in Finland was not a contractual breach and, having regard to Turner v Grovit, an anti-suit injunction was not just and convenient.
legal_issues: Whether the Brussels Regulation arbitration exception applied to the Club's English claim
Whether the Finnish court as first seised could determine arbitration exception questions
Whether New India was bound to pursue claims against the Club by arbitration in England
Whether an anti-suit injunction should restrain Finnish Insurance Contracts Act proceedings

confidence.notes: Long judgment with structured conclusions on Regulation, arbitration and injunction issues.

notes: Eady J awarded Galloway £150,000 after Telegraph defamation on oil-for-food allegations; Reynolds privilege and fair comment rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Galloway v Telegraph: £150,000 damages for Saddam payment libels
key_facts: The Daily Telegraph published articles in April 2003 alleging Mr Galloway received secret payments from Saddam Hussein via the oil-for-food programme.
Headlines included 'Galloway in Saddam's pay' and a leader describing the conduct as tantamount to treason.
The Telegraph did not plead justification; Galloway was not shown the Baghdad documents before publication and was not told personal enrichment would be alleged.
The defendant argued neutral reportage and Reynolds qualified privilege; Eady J found serious defamatory meanings and no privilege.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court defamation trial on meaning, privilege, fair comment, and damages after articles published during the Iraq war.
enrichment.outcome: Claimant succeeded; £150,000 general damages awarded for seriously defamatory publications and aggravating conduct; meanings included secret payments, diversion of oil-for-food funds, and conduct tantamount to treason.
enrichment.ratio: Publication of unverified Baghdad documents alleging personal enrichment of a public figure without prior opportunity to respond fairly cannot attract Reynolds qualified privilege or neutral reportage; where no justification is pleaded and allegations are grave, substantial damages are required to vindicate reputation.
legal_issues: Natural and ordinary meaning of Telegraph articles alleging payments from Saddam Hussein
Whether Reynolds qualified privilege applied to Baghdad document reporting
Whether neutral reportage protected publication of Iraqi documents
Whether fair comment defence succeeded
Appropriate level of general damages for unapologised grave libels

confidence.notes: Full trial judgment with detailed findings on meaning, privilege, and damages.

notes: Bennett J dismissed Thapa judicial review; work permit approval letter did not create legitimate expectation of leave to remain.

enrichment.short_title: Thapa v SSHD: no legitimate expectation from work permit letter
key_facts: Mr Thapa entered the UK illegally in 1999 and applied for asylum, which was refused; he appealed through Simman solicitors.
Work Permits UK approved a 36-month work permit in March 2003 but stated leave to remain would be considered separately.
On Malik & Malik's advice he withdrew his asylum appeal in April 2003; leave to remain was refused in February 2004 and removal to Nepal was directed.
He claimed a legitimate expectation from the work permit letter that he could remain, having relied on it to withdraw asylum proceedings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review limited to legitimate expectation after permission granted on that ground alone; earlier refusal of broader permission.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; work permit approval did not create a legitimate expectation of leave to remain; claimant to pay defendant's costs on standard basis.
enrichment.ratio: A Work Permits UK letter approving employment for 36 months while expressly stating that leave to remain would be considered separately cannot create a legitimate expectation of residence; the two-stage work permit and leave process and Immigration Rule paragraph 131 requirements are incompatible with treating permit approval as conferring leave.
legal_issues: Whether work permit approval created a legitimate expectation of leave to remain
Whether withdrawal of asylum appeal on mistaken legal advice gives rise to unfairness requiring grant of leave
Application of Coughlan third-category legitimate expectation in immigration context
Whether exceptional discretion outside the Rules should override immigration control
linked_authorities: R v North and East Devon Health Authority ex parte Coughlan [2001] QB 213

confidence.notes: Clear judgment on two-stage work permit process and Coughlan principles with agreed legal framework.

notes: Munby J on preliminary issue: capacity to marry is general not spouse-specific; experts should use E's solicitor's October 2004 questions.

enrichment.short_title: Sheffield v E: test for capacity to marry is not spouse-specific
key_facts: Sheffield City Council brought inherent jurisdiction proceedings over E, a 21-year-old woman with hydrocephalus and spina bifida alleged to function at a 13-year-old level.
E planned to marry S, a Schedule 1 offender with convictions for sexual offences against minors; the council sought to prevent marriage and association.
A preliminary issue arose whether capacity to marry S should be assessed in case-specific terms or as general capacity to understand marriage.
Dr M had been instructed under differing formulations in September and October 2004 letters.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Preliminary issue in inherent jurisdiction proceedings on the legal test and expert questions for assessing capacity to consent to marriage.
enrichment.outcome: Preliminary issue determined on written submissions; proper expert questions are those in E's solicitor's letter dated 6 October 2004; capacity is whether E can marry generally, not whether she can marry S specifically.
enrichment.ratio: Capacity to marry is whether a person understands the nature of the marriage contract and the duties and responsibilities normally attaching to marriage in 2004; it is not whether they have capacity to marry a particular person, and the court has no jurisdiction to assess whether marriage to a specific individual is wise or in best interests.
legal_issues: Whether capacity to marry is assessed generally or in relation to a proposed spouse
Whether best interests of marriage can be considered when assessing capacity
Whether Re MB-style capacity analysis applies to marriage
What questions should be put to psychiatric experts on capacity to marry
linked_authorities: In the Estate of Park deceased, Park v Park [1954] P 112
In re F (Adult: Court's Jurisdiction) [2001] Fam 38
Re S (Adult's Lack of Capacity: Carer and Residence) [2003] EWHC 1909 (Fam)
Masterman-Lister v Brutton & Co (No 1) [2002] EWCA Civ 1889

confidence.notes: Authoritative preliminary issue judgment with detailed historical analysis and clear conclusions at paragraph 141.

notes: Capewell carousel fraud receiver appeal; judgment ends with remittal directions on costs.

enrichment.short_title: Capewell v Customs: discharge of CJA 1988 receiver for carousel fraud
key_facts: Mr Capewell faced VAT carousel fraud charges; Customs appointed a receiver under section 77(8) CJA 1988.
Lindsay J refused discharge despite very high receiver costs relative to restrained assets.
Appeal concerned proportionality of receivership costs and whether restraint alone sufficed.
Court considered CPR 69.7 assessment procedure and Hughes principles.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against refusal to discharge a criminal receivership appointed in aid of restraint.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal partially succeeded; receivership discharge/remittal and costs issues remitted with detailed directions.
enrichment.ratio: Excessive receiver costs alone require assessment under CPR 69.7 rather than automatic discharge, but a judge must actively consider whether remaining prosecution concerns can be met by restraint alone; receiver remuneration must be proportionate to receivership objectives.
legal_issues: Grounds for discharge of a section 77 receiver
Proportionality of receiver costs in carousel fraud cases
Use of CPR 69.7 for receiver remuneration assessment
Costs consequences on partial success

confidence.notes: Core principles clear though published text ends during costs/remittal directions.

notes: Extradition appeal complete but judges metadata lists Lord Bingham and Lord Diplock.

enrichment.short_title: Raffile v USA: extradition appeal dismissed with liberty to apply on charges
key_facts: District Judge Pratt sent Raffile's case to the Secretary of State for extradition to the United States.
Appeal challenged delay, charge formulation, and refusal to adjourn the extradition hearing.
Section 82 passage-of-time bar and section 87 human rights issues were considered.
US government acknowledged charge amendment might be technical only.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal under section 103 Extradition Act 2003 with linked JR application refused.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; leave to apply for JR refused; liberty to apply within 14 days on outstanding US charge amendment issue; costs order for representation.
enrichment.ratio: Section 103 appeal power can address procedural unfairness including refusal to adjourn; section 82 requires actual injustice or oppression from delay; charge amendment issues may be pursued under liberty to apply rather than parallel JR where section 103 suffices.
legal_issues: Section 82 passage of time in extradition
Whether JR needed alongside section 103 appeal
Refusal to adjourn extradition hearing
Amendment of US extradition charges

confidence.notes: Dismissal and liberty to apply clearly stated.
